A 59-year-old man is assessed for sudden onset of left arm pain that began 7 days after hospitalization
for an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. He underwent percutaneous coronary angioplasty
and stenting of the distal left anterior descending artery. The pain, described as sharp, woke him from

sleep, and he now reports numbness in the fingers and difficulty moving the arm. His medical history
includes hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Current medications are atorvastatin, aspirin, lisinopril,
metoprolol, and clopidogrel. Vital signs include a temperature of 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse of 114/min,
respirations of 18/min, and blood pressure of 123/65 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.
Examination of the left arm reveals coolness, pallor, and absence of a palpable radial pulse. Muscle
strength is 1/5 in the left upper extremity and 5/5 in all other extremities. What is the most likely
underlying diagnosis? Answer Choices: (A) Iatrogenic brachial arterial injury (B) Brachial plexus
neuropathy (C) Acute aortic dissection (D) Stress-induced cardiomyopathy (E) Subclavian artery
stenosis (F) Compartment syndrome (G) Ventricular pseudoaneurysm (H) Left ventricular mural
thrombus (I) Post-stent thrombosis (J) Postmyocardial infarction syndrome
 A. Brachial plexus neuropathy
B. Postmyocardial infarction syndrome
C. Ventricular pseudoaneurysm
D. Acute aortic dissection
E. Compartment syndrome
F. Left ventricular mural thrombus
G. Iatrogenic brachial arterial injury
H. Stress-induced cardiomyopathy
I. Post-stent thrombosis
J. Subclavian artery stenosis
